questions.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed between the curves $y=2x$ and $y={x}^{2}$ above the line $y=2.$ What is ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA\,$ expressed as a repeated integral?
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/4e58d7969f0b31206ae8c3385a857c0ad6cf8a42ee79909d51c3a6b58a090852.png)

We need to represent $D$ as a type II region. Writing $y=2x$ and $y={x}^{2}$ in terms of $y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2} \\ y={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,x=\sqrt{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{y} & =\frac{y}{2} \\ y & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} \\ {y}^{2}-4y & =0 \\ y(y-4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, since our region lies above the line $y=2,$ the $y$-limits are 
$2\le y\le 4.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/16944d6651297f1c13c39ddf3d9160d721f5f29bfa6b0acac0db46c88295964e.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le y\le 4,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \sqrt{y}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{y/2}^{\sqrt{y}}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type II region. 

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3-{y}^{3} & ={y}^{3} \\ 2{y}^{3} & =3 \\ {y}^{3} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y$-limits are 
$0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}}.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/366146b42d476b8d2a467e607a3bba1ef65ddc8a344b3f0e17ee4652ccc0463a.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}},\,{y}^{3}\le x\le 3-{y}^{3}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{3/2}}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{3-{y}^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{3/2}}[{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{3-{y}^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dx]dy\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{{y}^{2}}(y-1)\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-1)[{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{{y}^{2}}\,dx]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-1)\,[x]_{{y}^{3}}^{{y}^{2}}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-1)({y}^{2}-{y}^{3})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-{y}^{4}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2})\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-{y}^{4}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={[-\frac{{y}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{y}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{30}\end{aligned}
$$

The integral is defined over a type II region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}{\int }_{0}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{y}dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}[x]_{0}^{y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}(y-0)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}y\,\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}y\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}\,dy & ={[\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-1-0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over a type II region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,2{y}^{2}\le x\le {y}^{2}+1\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}y\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}y\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[{\int }_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[\,x\,]_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y({y}^{2}+1-2{y}^{2})dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{3})\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{3})\,dy & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$
